blocks.text: Terrace Site Audit, Sunlight Mapping & Tool Safety Drill

You will investigate an approved school terrace or home balcony, map sunlight over the day, locate water and drainage points, and plan a small container area. You will learn to notice hazards, record measurements and handle a hand trowel safely. The teacher confirms school site clearance before students enter.
LOOK CLOSELY: Which features in this picture could help the team work safely? Point to two and explain your choices.

TEACHER CHECK • BEFORE ACCESS The teacher obtains school management’s site clearance, including competent assessment of roof capacity, barriers, access and drainage. A teacher’s activity signature records learning; it does not certify the building.
STUDENT CHECK • WITH SUPERVISION Observe the approved area, measure safe floor distances, record sunlight and report concerns. Do not lean over, climb on or reach above a boundary wall.

Equipment: clipboard, pencil, tape measure, compass, chalk, gloves, apron, hand trowel and practice tray. Use a clock for timed observations. Water is needed only for a teacher-led tray demonstration.
OBSERVER Notices sun, shade and hazards.
RECORDER Logs evidence and team decisions.
Rotate roles so everyone practises. Meet once to plan, then return at teacher-agreed times to observe sunlight.
BEFORE I BEGIN, I WONDER… Our classroom window casts a moving shadow. What might cause the shadow from a rooftop water tank to change during the day?
ACTIVITY 1 • FIVE STEPS TO A SITE PLAN

STEP 1 • CHECK BOUNDARIES FROM A SAFE PLACE Locate the boundary from the teacher-marked work area. Ask the teacher for the verified barrier height and site-access decision; record the source in your log. Practise vertical measurement on a safe indoor board if needed. Never reach to measure a terrace edge.

STEP 2 • MAP DIRECTIONS & SUNLIGHT Hold a compass level, away from metal objects, and locate north, east and south with help. Mark north on your sketch. At agreed times, record whether your chosen spot is in direct sun or shade and note clouds. Identify shadows from tanks, towers or trees. Never look directly at the sun.

STEP 3 • CHECK WATER ACCESS & DRAINAGE Locate the tap and drain from the safe area. Measure the route from tap to proposed containers in metres. Observe existing puddles or visible blockage without opening drains. If needed, watch the teacher use a little water in a tilted tray to model runoff; do not pour water across the walking area.

STEP 4 • INSPECT & PRACTISE WITH TOOLS Put on well-fitting gloves. Look for cracks, rust or a loose handle and report defects. The teacher checks attachment strength—do not pull the blade. Practise a comfortable grip and gentle scooping in a tray. Walk with the working end down; place the tool flat when you stop.

STEP 5 • MARK THE LAYOUT & COMPLETE YOUR LOG With permission, chalk a trial rectangle about 60 × 90 cm (roughly 2 × 3 feet). Keep paths and drains clear. The teacher sets safe clearance from boundaries and approves the load and placement. Measure the footprint, finish the log and explain one choice to the teacher.

SUNLIGHT TARGET • CHECK THE CROP Use 4–6 hours as a planning question, not a rule for every crop. Some cool-season leafy crops can grow with 3–5 hours of direct sun; many fruiting vegetables need 6–8. Your teacher checks the crop, season and local conditions.

DID YOU KNOW? • PLANTS RESPOND TO LIGHT Many shoots grow towards light. This is called phototropism. Predict what a seedling near a window might do. Check your prediction over several days; do not move heavy grow bags to test it.
MY REASONING: I would choose spot __________ because ___________________________

ACTIVITY 2 • BUILD A HOME FOR ROOTS
Soil-less Potting Mix Formulation & Grow Bag Setup

Prepare a lightweight growing medium, measure ingredients in equal parts and set up a grow bag for sowing. You will observe cocopeat as it absorbs water, blend a teacher-approved mix, and check how water moves through the filled bag. Your measurements will help you explain and improve your work.
AT THE END OF THIS ACTIVITY, I CAN…
HYDRATE & OBSERVE Follow the coir product instructions and describe changes in volume and texture.
MEASURE & BLEND Use equal-volume measures to make a 5 : 3 : 2 model mix, after teacher validation.
SET UP & CHECK Keep drainage openings clear, fill without hard packing, and record a supervised watering check.
5 PARTS • COCOPEAT Hydrated, fluffed and drained

Measure by volume using the SAME cup—not by mass. This is the model introduced earlier in the workbook; the teacher checks its suitability for the crop and available materials before use. Garden soil is not included in this soil-less version.
THINK BEFORE MIXING If one team packs its cups tightly and another fills them loosely, will their “five cups” be a fair comparison? Explain.
Five practical steps • Complete the log as you work
GET READY: approved site • gloves and apron • basin • labelled coir • mature vermicompost • perlite • equal cup • measuring jug • trowel • grow bag • catch tray • ruler • clock

STEP 1 • HYDRATE THE COCOPEAT Place the block in a basin with room for expansion. Read the product’s water and soaking instructions with the teacher. Add clean water gradually as directed, wait for softening, then gently break up clumps. Let excess water drain before measuring. Record water used and time; 4 L or 15 minutes will not suit every block.

STEP 2 • MEASURE & BLEND Using the same cup, loosely measure 5 parts prepared cocopeat, 3 parts mature vermicompost and 2 parts perlite. Level each measure without pressing. Mix gently until the ingredients are evenly distributed. Keep dusty materials low in the basin; the teacher prepares them to minimise dust.

STEP 3 • PREPARE THE GROW BAG Choose a crop-appropriate bag; a nominal 12 × 12 inch bag is only an example. Check seams, stability and drainage openings. A teacher handles any cutting or hole-making. If medium escapes through large holes, use permeable mesh that keeps water flowing. Do not add a gravel or husk “drainage layer”.

STEP 4 • FILL & LEVEL Put the bag in its approved position before filling. Scoop in the damp mix and tap the sides gently. Do not stamp or pack it hard. Leave about 3–5 cm below the rim for watering, adjusted to the container. Measure and record this gap. Ask a teacher to move a heavy filled bag.

STEP 5 • OBSERVE WATER MOVEMENT In a supervised area with safe runoff collection, add a measured amount of water slowly across the surface. Record the amount and when drainage is first seen. Stop and ask the teacher if water pools or the tray fills. Drainage time depends on the bag, mix and starting moisture; there is no universal 2–3 minute pass mark.

DID YOU KNOW? • A BYPRODUCT CAN HAVE A NEW USE Neem cake is material left after oil is extracted from neem seeds. It can be used as an organic amendment. It is not a guaranteed pest shield. Use it only if the teacher selects a suitable product and calculates its labelled rate for this batch—never a guessed handful or fixed 20 g.
FINISH SAFELY Avoid breathing dust, keep mix away from your face, and wash hands with soap afterwards. Empty collected drainage water as directed; do not leave the bag standing in runoff.
Container filling and drainage: University of Maryland Extension — https://extension.umd.edu/resource/planting-vegetables-containers
Measure carefully. Notice changes. Explain your result.

From a tiny seed to a carefully planned beginning

Investigate seed quality, plan a sowing pattern and plant a leafy crop in your prepared grow bag. Compare floating and sinking seeds as an experiment, then look for evidence of germination. Use the seed packet to choose depth and spacing, and water gently without disturbing your seeds.
AT THE END OF THIS ACTIVITY, I CAN…
INVESTIGATE SEEDS Record flotation observations and use a germination check to test my prediction.
MEASURE & SOW Follow crop-specific depth and spacing instructions using a ruler and blunt marker.
MIST & MONITOR Moisten the sowing zone gently, label the bag and keep a record of emerging seedlings.
MATERIALS CHECKLIST • CHECK WITH YOUR TEAM
Prepared grow bag with damp mix

Choose one locally suitable crop: fenugreek, spinach or coriander. Use organic seed if available; the teacher checks the packet, season and variety. Keep the main sowing batch separate from the small test sample.
PREDICT • CAN A FLOATING SEED STILL SPROUT? Write your prediction and one reason. Keep both groups so evidence can challenge your idea.

STEP 1 • OBSERVE FLOATING & SINKING Count a small sample of one seed type, such as 10 seeds, into clean water. Stir gently and observe after 2 minutes. Record how many float and sink; this is an observation, not a pass/fail test. Keep both groups on separate labelled damp paper towels. Put each in a clean covered container and check over the packet’s germination period. Keep conditions alike and record sprouts.

STEP 2 • PLAN & MARK THE SPACING Read the seed packet with your teacher: record sowing depth, seed spacing and any later thinning instructions. Gently level the damp growing mix. Use a ruler and blunt stick to mark rows or a grid. A 3 × 3 inch grid is only suitable if the crop guidance supports it. Count your planned sowing positions before planting.

STEP 3 • SOW AT THE CHOSEN DEPTH Use seeds from the main packet while the test sample is being observed. Mark the required depth on the blunt stick and make shallow holes or furrows. Place seeds as directed on the packet. Cover gently with fine, damp mix and lightly firm. Use 0.5–1 cm only when suitable for your chosen crop; different seeds need different depths.

STEP 4 • WATER WITH A FINE SPRAY Mist gently across the surface so seeds stay in place. Check with the teacher that the mix around the seeds is moist, not only its top skin. Pause to allow water to soak in. Avoid puddles, strong jets and a bag standing in runoff. Check moisture daily before adding water.

STEP 5 • LABEL, POSITION & LOG Label the bag with crop, variety, sowing date and team. Keep it in the approved spot with suitable temperature and light for the crop. Ask the teacher whether temporary protection from harsh sun is needed. Do not move a heavy filled bag yourself. Record the first emergence date, seedling counts and care decisions.

DID YOU KNOW? • A SEED CARRIES A STARTER KIT Inside a seed is a tiny plant embryo with stored food that supports early growth. Floating alone cannot tell us whether that plant will grow. Observing germination gives stronger evidence than judging a seed by where it sits in water.

SAFE HANDS • SAFE SEEDS Use teacher-approved untreated seeds. Never taste seeds or test sprouts. Keep markers below shoulder height, wipe up spills and wash hands with soap afterwards. Ask the teacher to handle any mouldy samples.
WORLD CONNECTION Use seed & water wisely
Sowing guidance: University of Maryland Extension — https://extension.umd.edu/resource/sowing-vegetable-seeds-outdoors
Record today’s setup. Return to observe what changes.

Total seeds tested: ______    Floating: ______    Sinking: ______ Do the two groups add up to the total?  Yes / Recheck Test start date: __________ Expected germination period (seed packet): __________________

Keep the test fair: use separate labelled towels, with the same moisture and location. If a group has no seeds, record 0 and “not tested”. Compare fractions when the group sizes differ. A small test cannot guarantee the whole packet’s result.
My result: ______ out of ______ seeds sprouted. My prediction was: Supported / Challenged / More evidence needed

Liquid feed & neem spray • Observe, choose, act and reflect
YOUR MISSION: Keep your crop healthy over four weeks. Check moisture, choose care with your teacher and record what changes. Today, discover why feeding roots and treating a pest are different jobs.
A • FEED THE ROOT ZONE Student applies teacher-prepared feed only with permission and suitable label guidance.
B • TEACHER-LED NEEM TREATMENT Teacher treats an identified pest when needed. Students stay outside the treatment area.
Two separate demonstrations. The photos illustrate actions; use the selected product’s label to decide equipment and protection.
Which picture shows liquid going to the growing mix?   A   B Which action needs an identified pest and teacher application?   A   B
Why should we check a plant before adding feed or spray? ______________________

DID YOU KNOW? • SMALL GARDENS CAN RECYCLE Microorganisms break down plant scraps into compost. Finished compost adds organic matter that helps soil hold moisture and nutrients. Recycling scraps and checking moisture before watering can reduce waste and conserve water.

CARE FOR PLANTS, PEOPLE & OUR SURROUNDINGS Use only the care needed, protect useful insects and keep runoff out of drains. Follow product labels, wash hands and wait for teacher harvest clearance. “Organic” does not mean every preparation is harmless.
Today I can:  Check before watering   Reuse suitable scraps as compost  Report an insect before treating it.  This helps because: ______________________
READY CHECK:  Activity 3 seedlings established   Site approved  Ruler, hand lens, water, gloves and notebook ready   Care rota agreed
Four practical steps • Daily checks and weekly measurements

STEP 1 • CHECK MOISTURE BEFORE WATERING With teacher permission, gently feel the mix about 2 cm below the surface, away from the stem and roots. Use a clean finger with intact skin, then wash hands; use a teacher-approved alternative if direct contact is unsuitable. Damp? Wait and recheck. Dry? Water slowly near the base until the root zone is moistened. Very wet or puddling? Stop and ask the teacher to check drainage. Tiny seedlings need shallower, gentler checks.

STEP 2 • LEARN WHEN LIQUID FEED IS NEEDED Review the crop, growing mix and plant health with the teacher; existing vermicompost may already supply nutrients. If feeding is needed, the teacher selects a labelled organic liquid feed suitable for this edible crop, measures and dilutes it as directed, and demonstrates application. Record product, dilution, amount and reason. More feed does not guarantee faster growth. Do not splash feed onto edible leaves.

STEP 3 • INSPECT FIRST, THEN DISCUSS NEEM Look at leaf tops and undersides with a hand lens. Record insects, spots or holes; do not assume every insect is harmful. Ask the teacher to identify the problem and consider monitoring or physical controls first. If neem is needed, a teacher selects a product labelled for this crop and pest, prepares and applies it according to its label. Students record from outside the treatment area. Do not use a fixed 5 mL/L recipe, add household soap or spray automatically every seven days.

STEP 4 • MEASURE THE SAME PLANT EACH WEEK Label one sample plant. At a similar time each week, hold a ruler vertically beside it: measure from the mix surface to its highest natural point without stretching leaves. Count fully opened true leaves, excluding the first seed leaves. Record height, leaf count, moisture, weather and care. If the sample is harvested or dies, record this; do not silently substitute a different plant.

DID YOU KNOW? • OIL AND WATER NEED HELP TO MIX An emulsifier helps spread oil into tiny droplets through water; it does not chemically break the oil down. A milky appearance does not prove a spray is safe or effective. Follow the selected formulation’s instructions for mixing and agitation.

TEACHER-LED CARE • PROTECT OUR FOOD CROP Follow label precautions, protective clothing, weather limits, return-to-area instructions and harvest waiting periods. Keep children and bystanders clear during spraying. Protect flowers, visiting insects and drains. Store products securely and wash hands after garden work.

ABOUT VERMICOMPOST TEA / JIVAMRUT: Discuss these farming practices, but do not brew or apply homemade preparations to this classroom food crop. This activity uses a labelled feed when needed; a 200 g / 2 L, two-hour brew is not an established universal recipe for safe, rapid growth.
HUMAN SERVICES CONNECTION: Why does the food team need our crop’s care record and teacher harvest clearance before serving the harvest?
Write what happened and why. “No treatment needed” is a valid result.

I COULD CARE FOR THE PLANT THIS WAY… Suggest one safe change to our care routine. What observation would tell us whether it helped?

Feed / neem decision recorded   Safe care explained   Ready for next review
Crop harvesting, yield weighing & micro-economics analysis

Harvest your leafy crop using a method suited to the plant. Weigh the usable greens, compare material costs with an estimated local market value, and present your evidence. Then hand suitable produce to the Human Services team and plan how clean plant scraps can return to the garden.
LOOK AT THE TWO ACTIONS: What must we protect while cutting? Why should the empty bowl be zeroed before weighing?
AT THE END OF THIS ACTIVITY, I CAN…
HARVEST WITH CARE Follow the teacher’s crop-specific method and protect the growing point if regrowth is intended.
WEIGH & CALCULATE Tare a scale, record net yield and calculate estimated value, cost recovery and ROI.
EXPLAIN & HAND OVER Present my portfolio and share the crop’s identity, weight and care record with the food team.

DID YOU KNOW? • LEAVE ROOM FOR ANOTHER HARVEST Spinach can produce more leaves after selective harvesting. Keep its centre and enough healthy leaves intact. Regrowth depends on crop, variety, weather and care; neither a fixed 1-inch cut nor a 10–12-day return suits every leafy crop.
Harvest background: University of Minnesota Extension — https://extension.umn.edu/garden-and-home/yard-and-garden/gardening-in-minnesota/growing-spinach-and-swiss-chard
BEFORE WE HARVEST How will our team protect the plant and keep the harvest clean?
Check the kit • Share the roles • Test the scale
MATERIALS CHECKLIST • ONE ITEM AT A TIME
Crop maturity and plant health checked
Any treatment harvest waiting period completed
Teacher has cleared this crop for harvest
CAPACITY AND DISPLAY STEP Capacity is the greatest mass the scale can hold. Resolution is its smallest displayed change. A “5 kg, 1 g” scale can hold up to 5 kg and shows changes in 1 g steps.
Our scale capacity: __________ kg     Display step: __________ g
The teacher checks the scale with a suitable known mass. Place the empty bowl on it and press Tare / Zero.
Display after tare: __________ g     Teacher check:  Ready   Recheck
SHARE THE WORK • ROTATE YOUR ROLES
PAUSE & EXPLAIN If we forget to tare the bowl, will the recorded crop mass be too high or too low? Why?
Work carefully. Record real measurements. Explain your choices.

STEP 1 • CHECK READINESS & HARVEST The teacher checks crop maturity, plant health and any treatment harvest interval. Wash hands and use clean tools. For spinach, selectively cut usable outer leaf stalks while protecting the centre; use teacher-confirmed guidance for fenugreek or coriander. Keep fingers away from blades. Place leaves gently in a clean tray. Separate damaged or contaminated material; do not taste during harvesting.

STEP 2 • TARE, WEIGH & LOG Set the scale on a firm, level surface. Place the empty bowl on it and press Tare / Zero. Add usable greens without exceeding capacity. Record the stable net mass in grams, using only the precision shown. Weigh before washing, or drain consistently and record the condition. Repeat for later harvests without counting the same produce twice.

STEP 3 • ITEMISE WHAT YOUR TEAM USED Record grow bags, potting ingredients, seeds and any feed or treatment used. Use receipts and actual quantities. Include cocopeat, vermicompost and perlite from our soil-less mix. Mark donated, reused and borrowed items. Charge purchased grow bags in full and consumables by the amount used; record borrowed tools separately. This simple comparison excludes labour and overheads, so it is not a complete business profit calculation.

STEP 4 • ESTIMATE VALUE & COMPARE COSTS Use a dated local price for the same crop and comparable quality. Record the source and whether it is organic or conventional; do not assume an organic premium. Convert grams to kilograms and calculate value. Market value estimates what the crop might be worth; it is not money received unless a sale occurred.

STEP 5 • PRESENT & HAND OVER Prepare a short Kaushal Mela explanation with your site map, mix record, sowing record, growth log and yield calculations. Explain one improvement and one benefit beyond money. Complete the food-team handover on page 38. Use photos for a later display if fresh produce cannot be kept safely; do not serve display produce without teacher clearance.
I COULD DO THIS ANOTHER WAY… How could we organise harvesting, weighing and recording so everyone practises safely? Describe your idea.
TRY THE MATHS • A PRACTICE EXAMPLE
Follow an example, then try your own idea
OUR EXAMPLE Material cost A = ₹100. Usable yield = 1,000 g. Comparison price = ₹150 per kg. These are practice numbers, not current market prices.
Estimated produce value is ₹50 more than material cost. This simple comparison excludes labour and overheads. Estimated value is not cash received unless a sale occurs.
YOUR TURN • WHAT IF WE HARVEST MORE?
Keep A = ₹100 and the price = ₹150/kg. Suppose usable yield becomes 1,200 g. Calculate the new value and estimated net return.
CAN THE RESULT ALSO BE NEGATIVE?
Yes. If B is less than A, net return and ROI are negative. If B equals A, ROI is zero. If A is zero, write “not applicable” for both percentages.
THINK BEYOND THE NUMBER A first harvest may not recover setup costs. What could we reuse, and what skills would we still have gained?
Use evidence for the money calculation and the learning reflection
Scale capacity: ______ kg  Smallest display step: ______ g  Tare checked:  Weighing condition:  Before washing   Washed and drained consistently
CHECK BEFORE YOU CALCULATE Which item could be reused for another crop? How could that affect future spending?
Use your recorded harvest and material costs.
Local comparison price: ₹______ / kg    Organic   Conventional
If A = 0, percentages are not applicable. Actual sales, if any: ₹______. Keep health and learning benefits separate from the rupee calculation.

MORE THAN MONEY • WHAT DID OUR GARDEN GIVE US? Vegetables contribute fibre, vitamins and minerals to a varied diet. Growing a crop helps us learn where food comes from and practise safe preparation. Harvest weight does not measure a personal health improvement or prove that organic food is more nutritious.

One way we reduced avoidable waste: _________________________________________

Work with Life Forms connects with Work in Human Services

FOOD-TEAM CHECK • BEFORE PREPARATION Teacher approves the crop, care record and treatment harvest interval. Use a clean food-safe container and arrange prompt suitable storage. Reject produce with animal contamination or decay. Wash suitable produce under safe running water before preparation; do not use soap. Check allergies and recipe suitability. Cooking Without Fire does not mean every garden leaf is suitable to eat raw.

Your evidence tells the story of your learning.

Harvest hygiene: University of Minnesota Extension — https://extension.umn.edu/food/preparing/cooking-at-home/washing-fresh-fruits-and-vegetables
Cocopeat — Hydrated, low-salt cocopeat forms a light, moisture-holding part of a teacher-selected mix.
Mature vermicompost — Well-finished compost contributes organic matter and nutrients. Do not use fresh manure.
Aeration material — Teacher-selected perlite or another suitable material helps maintain air spaces. Avoid breathing dust.
Grow bag or pot — A stable container with adequate drainage and enough room for the chosen crop.
Seeds and labels — Use reliable, labelled seeds. Record crop, variety and sowing date; follow the packet guidance.
Mixing and measuring tools — Tray, measuring cup and hand trowel help us measure equal volumes and mix neatly.
Watering can — A fine rose gives gentle watering. Check moisture before adding more water.
Protection and recording kit — Gloves, apron, ruler and scale; add a notebook and pencil for evidence.

activities.title: ACTIVITY 2 • BUILD A HOME FOR ROOTS
